name: Uma Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does an ordinary factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and run a soup-can filling machine at a food factory. I left after secondary school and still ask the lead operator to check my first fill weight after a changeover. I use an AI assistant every day to explain fault codes and draft the handover, then compare it with the machine book and actual cans. My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is typical for an operator, we have about three months of expenses saved, and some similar factories are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the AI handover helps me remember the fault, but the scale still decides whether the first soup can is full. A neat sentence cannot make an underfilled can heavier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The can line should keep paying its usual wage, and our three-month reserve gives us breathing space. The mortgage and two children still make me watch hours, but a small AI improvement is manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the filler, checking first cans with the lead and using the familiar AI fault explanation. I would add new money from each full paid month to our reserve after the mortgage and groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work continuing. I can use the small tool without pretending it changes a physical fill test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check on the first can?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I weigh three cans and check the seam before the tray is released. If one is light, I stop and ask the lead to check the filler valve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would set a small new transfer from each paid month after the usual bills. The three months already in the account are not a fresh contribution.

say: The **familiar** AI handover helps, but first cans still need weighing.
I would **keep** checking the can seam with the lead.
think: Our **three-month** reserve and some nearby factories make the plateau manageable.
A **mortgage** keeps me attentive to hours.
do: **Keep** running soup filler and weighing first cans with lead.
**Save** new money from full monthly wages after bills.
feel: **Calm** about paid work in the mild scenario.
S0.quote: A neat sentence cannot make an underfilled can heavier.
fieldNote: **Uma** uses AI daily for explanations but checks the can weight and machine book.
**Typical** pay, three months saved and some nearby plants support calm and new saving from wages.

steps.text: Keep running soup filler and weighing first cans with lead
Save new monthly wages after mortgage and groceries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift AI can plan ingredients faster, but a clean schedule must leave paid time to test a filler valve. I would ask the staff group to put the first-can check into any new target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If planning removes paid setup minutes, our usual wage could shrink. Three months saved help, but I do not want the reserve paying the mortgage because software made a rota look tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record four changeovers and bring the minutes to the staff group. If a paid stopped-line slot is offered, I would learn a new AI valve-warning control and test it against weighed cans; after repeated hour cuts, I would apply only to posted nearby operator roles whose pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a plausible weekly loss, but I can measure it and act. The new warning has to earn its place beside the scale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether it flags a light first can before the scale does, using ten safe stopped-line examples. A false green light would keep the physical weight check in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staff group ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask the plant to record paid setup and first-can checks in the rota. The time belongs on the clock, not in someone’s unpaid break.

say: I would **defend** paid first-can checks when AI shortens ingredient planning.
I would **learn** the new valve warning only in offered paid safe practice.
think: **Paid** setup minutes could disappear from my wage.
**Three** months saved give time, not an excuse for unpaid checks.
do: **Bring** four changeover records to staff group for paid setup time.
**Learn** new AI valve warning in offered paid stopped-line slot.
**Apply** after repeated cuts to posted nearby bill-covering operator job.
feel: **Anxious** about possible pay loss, with a way to respond.
S1.quote: The time belongs on the clock, not in someone’s unpaid break.
fieldNote: Her **progressive** view appears in a staff-group demand over paid inspection minutes.
**Learning** a genuinely new AI control is conditional on an offered paid stopped-line trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches ingredient plans in 2028 when I am forty-five, then capable hands-on robots reach can handling around 2031 when I am forty-eight. Robots could load, clear and inspect this filler with fewer operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large cut in routine can-line hours if that works, though I cannot know the plant’s exact decision. Three months saved and some nearby factories give us time to look, but not years of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts while asking for a fully funded, paid-time maintenance course with safe isolated-filler practice. If a posted nearby maintenance role accepts the certificate and pays our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; if hours fall first, I would apply to a posted nearby operator role at adequate pay and stop paid trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a major possible wage cut, with some cash and a route to test. I am frightened for the mortgage, but I can make calls before it becomes a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would maintenance practice cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fitter would isolate the can filler, let me test a faulty valve sensor and check the restart. My secondary schooling and operator practice are not a maintenance credential.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trip would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the paid weekend coach trip before touching school meals. It is a small saving, not a replacement wage.

say: 2028 **thinking** AI changes plans before can-handling robots around 2031.
I would **seek** paid safe training tied to actual nearby maintenance work.
think: **Routine** hours could fall sharply, but the plant decision is unknown.
**Three** months saved buy search time, not mortgage security forever.
do: **Enrol** in funded paid-time safe maintenance course for posted nearby adequate role.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted nearby maintenance job covering bills.
**Apply** after cuts to posted nearby adequate operator work and stop paid trips.
feel: **Anxious** about likely major risk, with several months to respond.
S2.quote: Three months saved and some nearby factories give us time to look, but not years of mortgage payments.
fieldNote: Her **moderate** cushion allows planning even though a large operator-hours cut is plausible.
**Maintenance** enrollment requires funding, paid safe practice, recognized qualification and a posted adequate local role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the staff group thinking AI reaches ingredient plans in 2031 when I am forty-eight, with capable can-handling robots around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five paid years can be used to qualify before the filler changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still worry routine hours may fall, but our three-month reserve can grow while I draw wages. I want a real posted job and paid training, not a certificate that sits in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the filler shifts and put fresh money from each full pay packet into our reserve. If a fully funded maintenance course gives paid safe practice and a posted nearby role accepts it at bill-covering pay, I would enrol and apply after qualification; I would ask the staff group to secure those paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a later pay cut, yet the lead time gives me more choices. I can build an option without leaving today’s wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the staff group into training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One junior asking for paid study can be ignored. Several operators asking together can put course hours into the schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is offered without paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working the filler and decline for now. The mortgage is due every month, and an unpaid day is a real loss.

say: **Paid** training should be available to all junior operators together.
think: **Routine** hours may shrink, but five paid years help.
A **funded** course must lead toward a real adequate local opening.
do: **Save** new money from full paid filler wages after bills.
**Enrol** in funded paid-time safe course for posted nearby adequate role.
**Apply** after qualification to posted nearby maintenance role covering bills.
feel: **Anxious** about later risk, with time to prepare.
S3.quote: I want a real posted job and paid training, not a certificate that sits in a drawer.
fieldNote: She **saves** genuinely new wages and uses the staff group to seek paid training time.
The **course** and later application preserve funding, paid safe practice, an accepted credential and adequate local vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches ingredient plans in 2036 when I am fifty-three, with capable can-handling robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. Ten years gives the children time to grow and the household time to build options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need wages after fifty-six, and our mortgage will not necessarily be gone. More warning helps only if I add to savings and find a qualification with a real employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the filler shifts and save a new amount from each full paid month. If offered a paid stopped-line slot, I would learn a new AI sensor-diagnosis control beyond today’s fault explanations; if a funded paid-time safe maintenance course and posted nearby bill-covering job exist, I would qualify and apply after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant robot date, though current income looks secure. I have time to test each step rather than guess our future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new diagnosis control add?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would compare valve faults across runs and suggest a sensor test, beyond explaining one code. I would check it with the fitter on a stopped filler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a maintenance job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first look for a posted nearby role that covers mortgage, travel and food. A distant offer must cover a family move before we consider it.

think: A **long** warning helps only with fresh saving and real nearby paid work.

S4.quote: I have time to test each step rather than guess our future.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** plan adds genuinely new AI diagnosis beyond routine daily fault explanations.
**Course** and application remain tied to funded paid safe practice and posted local adequate pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable can-handling robots around 2031 could cut hours before our mortgage is safer. Paid maintenance training and a real nearby job at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the time saved when a machine checks a can. I would like shorter weeks with the same pay if the plant can afford it, but I still weigh the first can myself. A scale tells the truth about a soup can before a report does.

headlineQuote: A scale tells the truth about a soup can before a report does.
portrait: **Uma**, forty-three, is a junior soup-can filler operator with secondary schooling and two school-age children.
She **uses** AI daily but checks first cans on a scale and asks the lead to verify changeovers.
**Typical** pay, three months saved and some nearby factories let her plan while a mortgage still matters.
She **works** with staff for paid inspection and pursues funded safe maintenance training tied to a posted adequate local job.
biggestWorry: **Fast** can-handling robots around 2031 could cut paid operator hours before the mortgage is safer.
whatWouldHelp: **Fully** funded paid-time maintenance training and a posted nearby bill-covering job would give Uma a route.
